Extracting text from documents
A document that looks simple on screen is rarely simple inside. The page a
reader sees is the result of many small drawing instructions, and the file
records those instructions in whatever order the producing program found
convenient. A library that wants the text back has to replay the instructions,
work out where every glyph landed, and only then decide which glyphs form
a word and which words form a line.
Speed matters because extraction is the first step of every pipeline that
follows. A retrieval system cannot index a page it has not read, and a
knowledge graph cannot link an entity it has not seen. When a collection
holds several million files, a difference of a few milliseconds per page
decides whether the whole job finishes overnight or runs for a week.
Correctness matters more than speed. A fast extractor that drops the accented
letters of a French contract, or joins two columns of a scientific paper into
one stream of nonsense, produces output that is worse than no output at all,
because nobody downstream can tell that something went wrong. The first
duty of the library is therefore to report what it could not read.
Fonts are the hardest part. The bytes in a text string are not characters. They
are codes that select glyphs in a font, and the mapping from code to character
can be given in three different ways, or not given at all. Some files carry a
table that maps every code to its Unicode value. Others name each glyph and
expect the reader to know that the name Eacute means a capital letter E with
an acute accent. Many old files rely on one of four standard encodings that
every reader is supposed to have built in.
Spacing is the second hard part. Most files contain no space characters
between words. The producing program simply moves the pen a little further
before the next word, and the reader has to notice the gap. To judge whether a
gap is a space, the reader must know how wide each glyph is, which again

depends on the font, on the font size, and on every transformation applied to
the page.
Damaged files are normal. A table near the end of the file says where every
object starts, and a single edit with the wrong tool makes that table wrong.
Good readers notice when an object is not where the table says and rebuild
the table by scanning the whole file. Users do not care why a file is damaged.
They care that the text comes out.
Hostile files are also normal. A stream of one hundred kilobytes can claim to
hold one hundred megabytes after decompression, and a page tree can refer to
itself. A library that runs inside a service must put a limit on every quantity
that the file controls: the depth of nesting, the size of a decoded stream, the
number of pages, and the time spent on any one of them.
Encryption is common in business documents, and most encrypted files open
with an empty password. The reader derives a key from values stored in the
file, checks that the key is right, and then decrypts each string and each
stream with a key of its own. When the check fails the reader must stop and
say that a password is needed. Guessing and returning noise is the worst
possible answer.
A page is more than a string of words. Headings, paragraphs, lists and tables
carry meaning that a language model can use, and a position on the page lets
an answer point back to its source. Even so, structure that the file does not
declare can only be estimated, and an honest extractor says which parts of its
output are declared and which are estimated.
Testing ties all of this together. Every defect gets a test before it gets a fix.
Every file in the test collection is compared with the output of an independent
reader, and the score for each file may rise but may never fall without a
written reason. Random input is thrown at every parser for hours, and any
input that causes a crash is kept forever as a regression test.

None of this needs anything beyond the standard library. Decompression,
hashing and the ciphers are all there. What remains is careful reading of the
specification, a large collection of real files, and the patience to treat every
strange file as a lesson and not as an annoyance.
The result is a small tool with one job: given a file, return what it says, where
it says it, and how sure we are.
